rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah fulfils the promise made to the believers in the previous sūrah.
rows.anchor: bears witness to the fulfilment of the promise made with the believers in verse 35 five of the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ḥudaybiyah truce prefigures the conquest of Makkah and the completion of God’s favour to the Prophet and his community.
rows.anchor: the truce of Ḥudaybiyah which proved to be a prelude to the conquest of Makkah and to the completion of favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah and Gospel predict the community’s conquest and dominance, showing that events unfold according to God’s prior plan.
rows.anchor: predictions and glad tidings of conquest and dominance of this ummah mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What has happened, is happening, and will happen is part of God’s certain scheme and cannot be stopped.
rows.anchor: whatever happened, is happening and will happen is not by chance. All this is pre-determined in the scheme of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah brought hope and news of clear victory when Muslims felt close to defeat; its promises and warnings materialized within two years.
rows.anchor: revealed as a ray of hope in very hopeless circumstances and as glad tidings of an open victory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 6 AH the Prophet dreamed he would perform ʿumrah with companions and summoned people to join despite the risk of Quraysh interference and battle.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) was given glad tidings in a dream that he will do ‘umrah with a group of his companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites tried to discourage Muslims and frighten them with the claim that those going to Makkah would never return.
rows.anchor: tried their best to discourgae and demotivate the Muslims. They tried to strike fear in their hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite the warning, Muslims trusted the Prophet’s dream and about fifteen hundred Companions prepared to go with him.
rows.anchor: Muslims fully trusted the dream of the Prophet (sws). For this reason, about fifteen hundred Companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historians differ whether the journey occurred in Rajab or Dhū al-Qaʿdah; both are months associated with pilgrimage, so Muslims expected Quraysh to respect them.
rows.anchor: There is a difference of opinion between historians about the month of this journey – whether it was Rajab or Dhū al-Qa‘dah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and Companions entered iḥrām for ʿumrah at Dhū al-Ḥulayfah, six miles from Makkah.
rows.anchor: wore the aḥrām of ‘umrah at Dhū al- Ḥulayfah, a place six miles from Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They brought seventy sacrificial camels and marked them with collars to identify them as offerings that should not be harmed.
rows.anchor: They took along with them seventy camels for sacrifice and to distinguish these animals, people put collars around their necks

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pilgrims carried no ammunition and only sheathed swords, taking care to give Quraysh no pretext for fighting.
rows.anchor: they did not have any ammunition with them; all they had were swords and they too were sheathed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh pride prevented them from letting the procession enter Makkah, but the Prophet blocked their efforts to provoke trouble.
rows.anchor: their over-blown pride of the age of jāhilliyah did not allow them to permit the procession to enter Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Ḥudaybiyah the Prophet sent an envoy to explain that he intended only to perform ʿumrah; Quraysh decided to kill him, but intervention saved his life.
rows.anchor: he had come with the intention of offering ‘umrah only; he has no other intention. However, they decided to kill the envoy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet then sent ʿUthmān, whom Quraysh treated respectfully and offered permission to circumambulate; he declined to do so without the Prophet.
rows.anchor: they even offered him to do ṭawāf if he wanted to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a rumour said ʿUthmān had been martyred, the Prophet called for a pledge to fight Quraysh, and the Companions eagerly pledged.
rows.anchor: a rumour spread in the Muslim camp that he had been martyred. Quite naturally, this acutely inflamed the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After hearing that Muslims were preparing to attack, Quraysh sent a delegation led by Suhayl ibn ʿAmr to negotiate peace.
rows.anchor: they sent a delegation under the leadership of Suhayl ibn ‘Amr to negotiate peace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh demanded that Muslims return and come back the following year, when Makkah would be vacated for three days for ʿumrah.
rows.anchor: to go back this year and return the following one whence the Makkans will vacate the city for three days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed asylum term required Muslims to return Quraysh fugitives while Quraysh would not have to return Muslim fugitives.
rows.anchor: if any person of the Quraysh ran away to the Muslims, the latter would be under obligation to return him whereas the reverse would not be the case

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The settlement established a ten-year truce forbidding either side from launching open or covert attacks.
rows.anchor: For ten years, there shall be no war between the two parties. During this time, no party will launch any open or hidden onslaught

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It required Muslims to return Quraysh fugitives while leaving Quraysh free not to return Muslims who defected to them.
rows.anchor: if a person belonging to the Quraysh ran away to the Muslims, they will have to return him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any Arab tribe could join the agreement as an ally of either party.
rows.anchor: Any tribe of the Arabs can enter into this settlement by becoming an ally of either of the two parties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims would return that year and perform ʿumrah the next, staying three days with one sword each while Makkans vacated the city.
rows.anchor: Muslims will go back this year and return the next to offer ‘umrah. They will be able to stay in Makkah for three days

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims found two terms detestable and interpreted acceptance as admitting defeat; ʿUmar expressed his anger and regretted his reaction for life.
rows.anchor: Two of these conditions were every detestable to the Muslims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the agreement, the Prophet ordered sacrifice and shaving to complete ʿumrah; when no one responded, he began himself, prompting the others to follow.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) directed the Muslims to offer sacrifice and then shave their heads

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The returning Muslims felt defeated and wondered about the Prophet’s true dream; the sūrah answered by announcing clear victory, with the tafsīr to explain how.
rows.anchor: a natural question that came to their minds was that if the dream of prophets of God are true, then what happened to the dream

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is promised clear victory through the Ḥudaybiyah truce, a prelude to Makkah’s imminent conquest and the completion of God’s favour upon him.
rows.anchor: open victory in the form of the Ḥudaybiyah truce.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After successfully completing his mission, the Prophet will attain God’s complete and eternal pleasure.
rows.anchor: complete and eternal pleasure of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The campaign opened a blessed way for believers’ faith to grow and for them to enter Paradise, which is great success in God’s sight.
rows.anchor: faith and to Paradise for the believers, which in the sight of God is great success

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The campaign brings God’s anger and condemnation on hypocritical men and women who make evil assumptions about God and fail to grasp that all heavenly and earthly forces obey His wise command.
rows.anchor: all the forces of heavens and the earth are under the command of God and He, in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger bears glad tidings and warnings, and people must believe in, respect, support, and help him; pledging to him is pledging to God, with reward for fulfilment and ruin only for the oath-breaker.
rows.anchor: Those who pledge a covenant at his hands, in fact, pledge a covenant at the hands of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Absent hypocrites will seek pardon by blaming household duties and ask the Prophet to pray for their repentance.
rows.anchor: the hypocrites who did not go out with him will come to him to beg pardon on the grounds that they were forced not to go

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their real motive was believing that the Prophet and Muslims would not return; this speculation ruined them, and forgiveness rests with God.
rows.anchor: the real reason for not going was their thought that this time the Prophet (sws) and the Muslims would not return

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When victory comes without war the hypocrites will seek to join the fighters; the Prophet must refuse, since declining a future campaign against a powerful enemy brings the same punishment as for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: when they will see that victory is being gained without any war, they will try their best to secure a place among the warriors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s excuse for missing battle is not hypocrisy if the person remains inwardly obedient to God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: Those people are mentioned whose excuse to not attend the battle would not be regarded as hypocrisy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The courageous Companions who made the pledge of Riḍwān receive glad tidings of victory, spoils, and the conquest of Makkah.
rows.anchor: The courageous among the Companions who took the bay’ah riḍwān are mentioned. They are given glad tidings of victory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had Quraysh fought at Ḥudaybiyah, they would have been routed.
rows.anchor: had the Quraysh waged war on the occasion of Ḥudaybiyah, they would have been routed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The agreement gave Muslims the upper hand and constituted an open moral and religious defeat for Quraysh.
rows.anchor: this truce was an open moral and religious defeat of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage also states the real reason Muslims were not permitted to fight despite Quraysh being overawed.
rows.anchor: the real reason because of which Muslims were not allowed to wage war

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims’ moral victory contrasts their piety and obedience with Quraysh’s emotional frenzy.
rows.anchor: In contrast with the bias of the Quraysh to emotional frenzy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s dream is affirmed, and the passage explains the wisdom behind its delayed fulfilment.
rows.anchor: An affirmation of the dream of the Prophet (sws). The wisdom in its delay to materialize is referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam’s supremacy over all religions is certain; the Torah depicts the Prophet and Companions, while the Gospel depicts truth’s gradual victory.
rows.anchor: The parable of the Prophet (rta) and his Companions (rta) found in the Torah and the parable of the gradual victory of the truth found in the Gospel
